upper_bound.quote: * (ii) there is $c>0$ such that $V \subseteq \{0, c\}$ with both values attainable.
upper_bound.witness: NON-SEQUITUR. What §3 establishes is only: the value set V contains at most one POSITIVE number (the argument in §3 begins 'Suppose V contains two distinct positive numbers c1 > c2 > 0' and never treats values c <= 0 other than 0). The text nowhere proves g(x) = f(x) - x >= 0; the only bound recorded is 'g(x) > -x'. Hence a priori V could be, e.g., {c, -δ} with c > 0 and some negative value -δ attained at some point, or contain several distinct negative values, none of which is ruled out by the §3 dichotomy argument. So the conclusion 'V ⊆ {0,c}' (and the alternative 'g ≡ 0') does not follow from what was proved. A proof of g >= 0 (e.g. iterating f(x) = x + g(x) > 0 along the orbit x, x+g(x), x+2g(x), ... which must stay positive) is missing from the text.
upper_bound.load_bearing: Everything after §3 (Lemma 1, the level sets S_0, S_c, and the covering argument) is carried out under the standing hypothesis V ⊆ {0,c}; in particular Lemma 1 uses 'b = g(z) ∈ {0,c} (because V⊆{0,c})'. Without excluding negative values the classification of g as a single constant for all x is not established.

parsed.notes: Identity f(f(x))=2f(x)-x and the orbit form g(x+g(x))=g(x) are derived correctly; verification uses QM-AM and AM-GM for x and y+c, covering both inequalities and all c>=0. The necessity argument (§3–§6) is largely correct but never excludes negative values of g, so the dichotomy V⊆{0,c} does not follow. Case-labeling in §7 is also sloppy.
